summary: This work develops an analytic theory of reservoir engineering for superconducting cavity cooling using gate-defined double-quantum-dot spin qubits as a tunable photon birth-death process. Lindblad simulations confirm millikelvin steady-state cavity temperatures achievable through collective bright-mode coupling in two-dot configurations, subject to constraints from memory effects, saturation, and dark-state formation.
motivation: Reaching millikelvin photon occupations in circuit-QED cavities improves qubit coherence and measurement fidelity, motivating active cooling schemes beyond passive dilution refrigeration.
method: The authors treat a gate-tunable DQD as an engineered reservoir rather than a spectroscopic probe, deriving closed-form expressions for cavity steady state by mapping gate control of populations, coherences, linewidths, and detuning onto an effective photon birth-death process with detailed balance. Lindblad simulations validate the framework in realistic parameter regimes.
result: Cavity refrigeration below both the bath temperature and DQD setpoint is possible, with two-dot bright-mode coupling enhancing cooling beyond single-dot limits, though dephasing and gate-voltage mismatch limit performance in experimental implementations.
